weaknesses: Dataset correctness is insufficiently validated. Millions of graphs are produced using single-precision root solving, a global threshold, skeletonization, and heuristic node merging, while validation consists only of visual checks on unspecified hundreds of examples. The authors acknowledge missed low-DOS edges and component fragmentation but provide no measured failure rate, exact-diagonalization error metric, resolution-sensitivity study, or quality breakdown by band number and hopping range. Consequently, the reliability of the central artifact is unknown.

The experiments do not establish that spatial edge geometry or multiedges create the reported difficulty. There is no comparison against collapsed simple graphs, topology-only inputs, raster/CNN baselines, geometry-aware models, curve encoders, or dedicated multigraph methods. It is also unclear how the 13-dimensional edge features are consumed by each nominally standard GNN layer. Thus the conclusion that existing GNNs struggle specifically with geometry-aware multiedge learning is unsupported.

Evaluation is incomplete for a benchmark paper: only three variants are tested, the full HSG-12M, three-band, and temporal datasets receive no baseline, and all models are trained for an arbitrary five epochs without convergence or tuning analysis. The temporal resource in particular has suggested tasks but no formal split, metric, or empirical baseline.

Random graph-level splits are problematic because samples form a dense Cartesian grid within each polynomial family and most of HSG-12M consists of topologically isomorphic or smoothly adjacent examples. Near-duplicate parameter neighbors can therefore cross train/test boundaries. Parameter-blocked and extrapolation splits, nearest-neighbor baselines, and cross-class duplicate/isospectral collision analyses are needed. Moreover, the sampled coefficient grid includes zero, where a nominally defining monomial disappears and the family label may become unobservable or conflict with another class.

The target definition is internally unclear. Appendix A defines a characteristic-polynomial class only through binary support over powers of z, which discards the powers of E inside each coefficient, whereas dataset construction appears to vary those E powers to obtain 275 and 1102 multi-band classes. The precise class enumeration, duplicate-removal rule, and equivalence relation are therefore not reproducible from the manuscript as written.

Several impact claims are overstated. A nonunique Toeplitz factorization of an arbitrary matrix produces a nonunique collection of graphs, not a well-defined topological fingerprint. Likewise, claims about material discovery and inverse design are not supported by any physical-property task or validation on realistic materials; the benchmark only predicts synthetic generator-family identifiers.

The broad claim of being the first generic large-scale multigraph dataset is not adequately positioned against knowledge graphs, interaction/temporal multigraphs, multiplex networks, and road-network resources. The more defensible novelty is specifically a large graph-level dataset with continuous parallel-edge geometry. Dataset size alone is also a weak diversity argument because the 11.6 million examples are generated by dense sampling of only 1401 templates, with little statistical analysis of effective diversity.

Random stratified splitting is poorly suited to a dense Cartesian coefficient grid. Nearby parameter points and potentially near-identical or isomorphic graphs can occur across train and test sets; even HSG-topology removes isomorphisms only within each class. No coefficient-block, extrapolation, family-held-out, or cross-class deduplication split is evaluated.

The coefficient grids apparently include zero. When a designated free coefficient becomes zero, its support-defining monomial disappears, so samples nominally assigned to different characteristic-polynomial classes can collapse to the same lower-support polynomial with inconsistent labels. This potential cross-class collision is neither audited nor discussed.

The experiments do not establish that spatial multi-edge geometry is responsible for performance. There are no ablations that collapse parallel edges, remove coordinates or DOS features, compare topology-only inputs, or encode the released edge polylines. GINE-versus-GIN is not a controlled feature ablation, while the best-performing GraphSAGE baseline does not consume the stated edge features, weakening the paper's central interpretation.

The training protocol confounds dataset difficulty with optimization. At 1,000 steps and batch size 6,000, HSG-12M receives only about 0.65 to 1.3 passes through its training set depending on unspecified DDP batch semantics, whereas smaller subsets receive many passes. Convergence curves, meaningful hyperparameter tuning, and the checkpoint-selection rule are absent.

T-HSG-5M is presented as a major contribution but receives no temporal benchmark. Sequence lengths, overlap, split construction, and leakage prevention are insufficiently documented; the sequences appear to reuse the same static coefficient-grid samples along many overlapping trajectories.

The claimed coverage of realistic Hamiltonians is unsupported: the construction varies only two coefficients within a restricted template. The assertion that varying a z^0 term has no effect on the spectral graph is generally false; even an additive constant can translate the spectrum, and for multiband polynomials it can deform its geometry or topology.

The claimed universal 'topological fingerprint' for arbitrary matrices is not technically justified. Toeplitz factorizations are non-unique, a minimum-cardinality factorization need not yield a unique multiset, and neither injectivity, stability, nor a canonical computation is proved. Treating vectors as polynomial coefficients is likewise an arbitrary encoding rather than a demonstrated fingerprint.

The inverse-material-design claims substantially exceed the evidence. Characteristic-polynomial support does not uniquely determine microscopic hopping structure, and the paper itself notes that z exponents encode composite paths. High Top-10 accuracy on random splits of synthetic data does not validate inference for real materials or out-of-distribution spectra.

The reported five-order-of-magnitude speedup compares only one bottleneck against prior code, without sufficient hardware, precision, accuracy-matching, memory, or end-to-end runtime details. Moreover, the release and dataset URLs are blank in the manuscript, so the claimed artifacts cannot presently be verified.
